title: Packaging and Distributing CLI Tools
subtopics: Testing CLI behavior in multiple environments
learning_outcomes: Describe npm package configuration and explain how it relates to Packaging and Distributing CLI Tools.
Demonstrate Executable entry points in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Versioning.

content.intro: Packaging and Distributing CLI Tools is part of command line applications. This lesson connects npm package configuration, Executable entry points, Versioning to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: npm metadata and lockfiles make dependencies and project tasks repeatable across machines. Install from the lockfile in a clean checkout and run tests after dependency changes.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: npm metadata and lockfiles make dependencies and project tasks repeatable across machines. Keep direct dependencies intentional, commit the lockfile, review lifecycle scripts, and audit updates.

items.title: npm package configuration
items.text: npm metadata describes project scripts and dependencies; lockfiles improve repeatability but do not guarantee a dependency is safe.

items.title: Testing CLI behavior in multiple environments
items.text: Tests should assert observable behavior and include failure cases. Deterministic inputs and cleanup are more valuable than depending on network state or exact timing.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Packaging and Distributing CLI Tools. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with npm package configuration; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Executable entry points, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating semver ranges or an audit report as a guarantee that a dependency is safe.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Review provenance, release notes, transitive dependencies, and behavior before upgrading.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
